slide.title: Start With the Destination
slide.body: A dotted path runs backwards from a teal map pin 'Outcome' through 'Evidence' to 'Activities'. Small tag: AI for Educators and Trainers · Lesson 5.

scenes.voiceover: Have you ever finished a lesson where the activities were fun, the learners were busy, and yet you could not say what they had actually learned? A clear outcome at the start of planning prevents that. It also makes AI much more useful.

slide.title: Planning Lessons with Clear Outcomes
slide.body: AI for Educators and Trainers · Lesson 5 of 12 · Week 2: Designing Lessons and Materials

scenes.voiceover: Welcome to week two, where we design lessons and materials. Many educators start planning with activities. I will do a group discussion, then a video. A stronger method is to start from the learning outcome and work backwards. This is sometimes called backward design.

slide.title: Step 1: Write the outcome
slide.body: Observable verbs (tick): calculate · explain · handle · compare. Verbs you cannot see (cross): understand · know.

scenes.voiceover: Step one, write the outcome. What will learners be able to do at the end? Use an action verb you can observe, like calculate, explain, handle or compare. Avoid verbs you cannot see, such as understand or know.

slide.title: Backward design
slide.body: Three boxes, arrows pointing right to left in planning order: 1 Outcome → 2 Evidence (role-play, 3 questions, exit ticket) → 3 Activities that prepare for the evidence

scenes.voiceover: Step two, decide the evidence. How will learners show they have reached the outcome? This is your check for understanding, such as a short role-play, three questions, or an exit ticket. Step three, plan the activities. Every activity should prepare learners for that evidence.

slide.title: How AI helps
slide.body: Vague aim → observable outcome · Ideas for checks for understanding · Activity sequence with timings. Format: Step | Minutes | Educator | Learners

scenes.voiceover: AI can help at each step. It can turn a vague aim into an observable outcome, suggest ways to check understanding, and propose activities with timings. A useful format is a table with the step, the minutes, what the educator does, and what learners do.

slide.title: You adapt the plan
slide.body: Real timings · Local examples · Remove equipment you do not have · Add support for learners who need it

scenes.voiceover: But AI does not know your room, your group or your limits. So you adapt its plan. Adjust timings to your real group, replace examples with ones from your context, remove anything that needs equipment you do not have, and add support where learners need it.

scenes.stock_query: traveller checking destination on phone map
scenes.voiceover: Backward design is like planning a journey. You choose the destination first, then decide how you will know you have arrived, and only then choose the roads.

scenes.on_screen_text: AI suggests. You check the route.
scenes.voiceover: An AI assistant is like a route planner. It suggests good roads quickly, but it does not know that one bridge is closed today. You check the route against what you know.

scenes.stock_query: corporate trainer leading small workshop group
scenes.voiceover: Let's move from the classroom to the workplace. Tomás is a corporate trainer at an insurance company in Madrid, in Spain. He must run a sixty-minute workshop for new customer-service staff on handling complaints.

slide.title: Outcome and evidence
slide.body: Outcome: respond to a complaining customer in 4 steps → Listen · Acknowledge · Solve · Confirm. Evidence: 3-minute role-play + checklist.

scenes.voiceover: He writes his outcome first. Participants can respond to a complaining customer in four steps: listen, acknowledge, solve and confirm. His evidence is a three-minute role-play, marked with a checklist.

slide.title: The AI's plan
slide.body: Table: Opening question 5 min · Model 4 steps 10 min · Practice with scripts 15 min · Role-play in threes 20 min · Review 10 min

scenes.voiceover: Then he prompts the AI with the four parts from lesson two. Twelve new staff with no customer-service experience, his outcome, sixty minutes in one room with no projector, and a timed table plus a checklist. The AI suggests five steps. An opening question, a model of the four steps, practice with scripts, a role-play in groups of three, and a review.

slide.title: Three changes
slide.body: 1. Retail examples → insurance situations (invented details) · 2. 5 minutes moved from the opening to the role-play (now 25 min) · 3. Printed four-step card for extra support

scenes.voiceover: Tomás makes three changes. He replaces the AI's retail examples with insurance situations, like a delayed claim, with every customer detail invented. He moves five minutes from the opening to the role-play, because his groups need more practice. And he adds a card with the four steps, for people who struggle to remember a sequence under pressure. The plan now fits his outcome, his time and his learners.

scenes.on_screen_text: Does it lead to the evidence?
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is to keep attractive activities that do not lead to the outcome, like a poster task when the outcome is a spoken conversation. Ask one question of every activity. Does this help learners produce the evidence I planned?

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Outcome → Evidence → Activities. 2. AI drafts outcomes, checks and timed plans fast. 3. Adapt timings, examples, equipment and support.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, start from an observable outcome, then decide the evidence, and only then plan the activities. Second, AI can suggest outcomes, checks, activities and timings quickly, especially in a timed table. Third, always adapt the plan to your context, and remove activities that do not lead to the outcome.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, write one observable outcome for a lesson you will teach soon, and use AI to draft a timed plan. Describe your learners as a group, with no personal data. Then change at least three things to fit your learners. It takes about thirty minutes. In the next lesson, we look at differentiating materials for different learners. See you there.
